  function initializeReadingPreferences() {

      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ádám Kovács
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>KR Labs
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">kovacs@krlabs.eu</span></a>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><a href="https://github.com/KRLabsOrg/squeez" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/KRLabsOrg/squeez</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Coding agents repeatedly consume long tool observations even though only a
small fraction of each observation matters for the next step. We study
<em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task-conditioned tool-output pruning</em>: given a focused query and one tool
output, return the smallest verbatim evidence block the agent should inspect
next. We introduce a benchmark of 11,477 examples built from SWE-bench
repository interactions and synthetic multi-ecosystem tool outputs, with a
manually curated 618-example test set. We fine-tune Qwen 3.5 2B with LoRA and
compare it against larger zero-shot models and heuristic pruning baselines. Our
model reaches 0.86 recall and 0.80 F<sub id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">1</sub> while removing 92% of input
tokens, outperforming zero-shot Qwen 3.5 35B A3B by 11 recall points and all
heuristic baselines by a wide margin.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para"><img src="2604.04979v1/squeez_mascot.png" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:67/65;" width="67" height="65" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Coding agents work over streams of file reads, grep hits, stack traces, build
logs, API responses, and version-control history
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In such observations, only a
small fraction of the tokens is relevant to the next decision, yet the agent
often has to re-read the entire output. This makes pruning a central efficiency
problem for agent systems
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hwang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kerboua et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We study a narrow but practical version of this problem: given a focused query
and a single tool observation, return the smallest verbatim evidence block the
agent should inspect next. The task is not to solve the issue from one
observation, but to preserve the relevant evidence and discard the rest. This
distinguishes our setting from generic prompt compression and from
document-level retrieval compression, which typically operate on prose
documents or retrieved passages rather than mixed-format tool output.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We make three contributions. We formulate task-conditioned tool-output
pruning as a benchmark task for coding agents, release a dataset spanning real
SWE-bench repository interactions and synthetic multi-ecosystem tool outputs,
and show that a compact Qwen 3.5 2B model fine-tuned for this task
substantially outperforms larger zero-shot models and simple heuristic
baselines. Because the model can be served through vLLM or used as a CLI
filter on piped tool output, it can be inserted into existing coding-agent
stacks such as <a href="https://openai.com/codex/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Codex</a> or
<a href="https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Claude Code</a>
with minimal changes to the surrounding agent loop. The
<a href="https://huggingface.co/KRLabsOrg/squeez-2b" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">model</a>,
<a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/KRLabsOrg/tool-output-extraction-swebench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">dataset</a>,
and <a href="https://github.com/KRLabsOrg/squeez" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">evaluation code and CLI</a>
are publicly available under the Apache 2.0 license.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt compression methods such as LLMLingua <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and
LongLLMLingua <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> compress long prompts before
generation. LLMLingua uses a coarse-to-fine compression pipeline with a budget
controller and iterative token removal, while LongLLMLingua adapts compression
to long-context settings with query-aware compression and document reordering.
These methods target prompt efficiency at the token or prompt-block level
rather than query-conditioned extraction from a single mixed-format tool
observation. Abstractive summarization addresses a different problem again,
since it rewrites salient content rather than preserving verbatim source
evidence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">See et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and Lapata, 2019</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Document-level context pruners are closer to our work. EXIT
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hwang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> performs extractive compression for
retrieval-augmented generation by selecting relevant portions of retrieved
textual context for a downstream question-answering stage. Provence
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chirkova et al., 2025</a>)</cite> formulates context
pruning as sequence labeling, combining pruning with reranking, and training on
diverse QA domains to obtain robust out-of-the-box RAG pruning. Open-source models such as Zilliz Semantic Highlight <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zilliz, 2025</a>)</cite>
adapt this idea to lightweight semantic highlighting, producing token- and sentence-level
relevance scores over retrieved documents for real-time highlighting. These
systems, however, assume retrieved passages or document text. They do not
target the mixed observations that arise in coding agents, where code, logs,
shell traces, metadata, and structured outputs are interleaved in a single
artifact.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our setting is also related to agent-specific pruning. FocusAgent
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kerboua et al., 2025</a>)</cite> reduces the context available to web agents by trimming
web observations, while SWE-Pruner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> targets coding
agents more directly by pruning repository code context. The nearest of these
to our work is SWE-Pruner, but its emphasis is repository-level code context
rather than single tool observations spanning files, logs, build outputs, and
other non-code modalities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, our task is related to extractive QA and supporting-evidence
supervision, where outputs are grounded in explicit spans or sentence sets
rather than free generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rajpurkar et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thorne et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Verbatim evidence extraction has also been applied in
domain-specific QA, where lightweight extractive pipelines select grounded
sentences to prevent hallucination <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kovacs et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The common
concern is faithfulness: outputs should remain traceable to source evidence.
Our setting differs in focusing on query-conditioned pruning of tool
observations rather than answer production from prose documents.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S2.F1.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="523.39" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 565.8 523.39" width="565.8"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="translate(0,523.39) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(282.91,0) translate(0,442.27)"><g stroke-width="0.4pt"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#F9F9F9;" fill="#F9F9F9" stroke="#000000"><path d="M 278.47 80.85 L -278.47 80.85 C -280.77 80.85 -282.63 78.99 -282.63 76.7 L -282.63 -76.7 C -282.63 -78.99 -280.77 -80.85 -278.47 -80.85 L 278.47 -80.85 C 280.77 -80.85 282.63 -78.99 282.63 -76.7 L 282.63 76.7 C 282.63 78.99 280.77 80.85 278.47 80.85 Z M -282.63 -80.85"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -274.32 63.05)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:39.65em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:9.8em;font-size:10pt;" height="145.1" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.49)" width="548.64"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

output, then derives a generative training target. At evaluation, predicted

</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Task Definition</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> illustrates the overall pipeline.
The benchmark input is a pair <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(q,o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(q,o)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> is a short task-conditioned
extraction query and <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math> is one raw tool observation. The output is a set of
one or more contiguous spans over <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y=\{(s_{1},e_{1}),\dots,(s_{k},e_{k})\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y=\{(s_{1},e_{1}),\dots,(s_{k},e_{k})\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where each span refers to line indices in the original output.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The task is intentionally narrower than bug solving. The model is not asked to
infer the correct patch from one observation, but to extract the minimal
evidence block that would help an agent on the next reasoning step. Queries are
short, concrete, and tool-aware. They may be easy, medium, or moderately
semantic; they need not avoid lexical cues if those cues reflect the underlying
agent need. The key requirement is that they define a plausible pruning
decision rather than a full diagnosis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Dataset</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Data Sources</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark draws on two sources of raw tool output.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">SWE-bench derived.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We clone repository snapshots from SWE-bench
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and execute 14 tool types against them —
file reads, grep, Git log and blame, test runners, linters, type checkers,
pip install, curl, and others — collecting 10,713 raw observations that
reflect the kind of output a coding agent encounters during issue resolution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Synthetic multi-ecosystem.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To extend coverage beyond SWE-bench’s Python-heavy distribution, we use
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">openai/gpt-oss-120b</span> to generate 2,039 realistic tool outputs for
representative tasks in TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, Docker, Terraform,
Kubernetes, and related build or deployment workflows. We also
construct 575 explicit negative examples by pairing mismatched queries and
tool outputs, where the correct pruning decision is to return nothing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The released benchmark contains 11,477 examples in total:
9,205 SWE-derived, 1,697 synthetic positives, and 575 synthetic
negatives, covering 27 tool types;
Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Curation and Statistics ‣ 4 Dataset ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> lists the tool-family counts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Example Construction</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each example pairs one focused query with one raw tool observation. Both
sources go through the same two-stage teacher-labeling pipeline using
<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">openai/gpt-oss-120b</span>. Given the background task and the raw tool
output, the teacher first writes a focused, tool-aware extraction query:
not the full issue statement, but a narrower local information need such as
finding the failure block, the relevant code region, or the commit entry that
matters for the next debugging step. It then selects the smallest contiguous
span or set of spans that answers that query.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The teacher sees a numbered rendering of the tool output for stable span
selection, but the released labels are always mapped back onto the original
raw text, so every target is a verbatim subset of the source. Positive
examples whose query cannot be supported by the observation are discarded.
For generative training, gold spans are linearized as XML-wrapped extracted
text, while the released benchmark stores the span coordinates over the
original tool output.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Curation and Statistics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We split SWE-derived examples by repository and synthetic examples by tool
family, yielding 10,508 training examples, 240 development examples, and 618
test examples. The held-out set was manually curated: from 729 candidate test
examples, 111 (15.2%) were excluded as near-duplicates, trivial 1–2 line
outputs, overly broad spans, or incorrect annotations. The final released test
set therefore contains only manually reviewed examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.3 Curation and Statistics ‣ 4 Dataset ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the source composition of the released
benchmark. Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Curation and Statistics ‣ 4 Dataset ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the largest tool families. The
distribution is intentionally heterogeneous: the benchmark mixes very short
observations such as Python exceptions and test summaries with long file reads,
type-check outputs, and container logs. This variation is one reason simple
truncation and lexical retrieval are weak baselines: relevant evidence may
occur at the beginning, middle, or end of the observation, and the useful
pruning unit depends on the tool type.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Model and Evaluation</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our model is Qwen 3.5 2B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026</a>)</cite> fine-tuned with LoRA
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. The model receives the focused query and
raw tool output and is trained to emit the verbatim extracted text wrapped in
<span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;relevant_lines&gt;</span> tags. We fine-tune for three epochs with maximum
sequence length 20,000, per-device batch size 8, gradient accumulation 4,
learning rate <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, warmup ratio 0.05, and weight decay 0.01. For
serving we merge the LoRA adapter into the base model and run the merged
checkpoint with vLLM. Training was performed on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We choose Qwen 3.5 2B because the Qwen 3.5 family offers strong performance on
code, reasoning, and agent benchmarks while providing small-scale variants
suitable for efficient deployment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026</a>)</cite>. In our setting, the aim is not to maximize
zero-shot reasoning depth with the largest possible generator, but to learn a
narrow supervised extraction policy that can run cheaply inside existing agent
systems. A 2B backbone is therefore a better fit for this use case than a much
larger decoder, while still remaining strong enough to benefit from
task-specific supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We compare against three zero-shot generative baselines — Qwen 3.5 35B A3B,
Kimi K2, and the unfine-tuned Qwen 3.5 2B base — and four simple heuristics:
BM25, First-N, Last-N, and Random. The heuristic baselines keep approximately
10% of the input lines so that they operate at a compression level similar to
the gold annotations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The matching unit is the <em id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">line</em>. Given a predicted line set <math id="S5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> and a gold
line set <math id="S5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math>, we report recall, exact match, compression, and two overlap
scores. In the main text, F<sub id="S5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_sub">1</sub> denotes a tolerant line-matching score in which
a predicted line matches a gold line if fuzzy substring similarity exceeds
0.5, reducing brittleness from minor formatting differences in generative
output. We also report strict exact-text overlap F<sub id="S5.p4.1.3" class="ltx_sub">1</sub> in
Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Setup. ‣ 6 Results ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> for completeness. Our analysis focuses on
<span id="S5.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">recall</span> under strong <span id="S5.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">compression</span>, with F<sub id="S5.p4.1.6" class="ltx_sub">1</sub> as the summary
metric. This reflects the task itself: dropping relevant evidence is usually
more harmful than keeping a slightly larger block.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, the model is intended as a lightweight pre-processing step for
agent systems. In our release it is exposed both as a CLI that can consume
piped tool output and as a vLLM-served model, so existing coding agents can
insert pruning before the next reasoning step without changing their core
planning logic.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All models are evaluated on the held-out 618-example test set. All generative
models receive the same <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;query&gt;/&lt;tool_output&gt;</span> prompt format as the
fine-tuned model. The fine-tuned model is served with vLLM; the larger zero-shot
models are accessed via OpenAI-compatible APIs.</p>
</div>

<span id="S6.T5.2.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Adjacent over-selection</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S6.T5.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.25pt 3.0pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.2.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:119.5pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.2.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.T5.2.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">build_output</span>, 110 lines. Query asks for the Dockerfile syntax error on line 12.</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S6.T5.2.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.25pt 3.0pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.2.5.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:91.0pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.2.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Finds the Dockerfile error but also includes a nearby Python <span id="S6.T5.2.5.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SyntaxError</span>.</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S6.T5.2.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.25pt 3.0pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.2.5.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S6.T5.2.5.4.1.1" class="ltx_p">Qwen 35B misses the Dockerfile error entirely and selects only the Python block.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Representative held-out examples. The fine-tuned model is strongest on
precise hits, compact failure blocks, and true negatives; its residual errors
are usually adjacent over-selection.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Squeez-2B attains the highest recall among all systems while maintaining
92% compression. It outperforms the 18<math id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger Qwen 3.5 35B A3B by
11 recall points and the unfine-tuned 2B base by 33 points. The gain is not
just recall: the fine-tuned model is also the most precise system in the
comparison, which indicates that it has learned a tool-specific extraction
policy rather than generic instruction following.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The zero-shot baselines differ in how they fail. Qwen 35B is the strongest of
them, but still misses benchmark-specific regularities: in repetitive logs or
Git history it often selects a semantically adjacent but incorrect block.
Kimi K2 is the most aggressive compressor, but pays for that with lower
recall, often dropping lines that look boilerplate-like but are actually part
of the gold evidence. The unfine-tuned 2B base under-compresses and produces
noisier extractions. Heuristic baselines perform substantially worse than any
generative model. BM25, which is effective for document retrieval, reaches
only 0.22 recall on tool output. This is a direct consequence of the task:
relevant lines may occur at the beginning, middle, or end of an observation,
and usefulness depends on the query rather than lexical overlap alone.
Figure <a href="#S6.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Setup. ‣ 6 Results ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the recall–compression trade-off across all
systems.</p>
</div>

</div>
        
<figure id="S6.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Recall–compression trade-off on the held-out test set.
<math id="S6.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000CC;" mathcolor="#0000CC">∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> Squeez-2B, <math id="S6.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#B30000;" mathcolor="#B30000" mathvariant="normal">■</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\blacksquare</annotation></semantics></math> Qwen 35B, <math id="S6.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacktriangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#CC6600;" mathcolor="#CC6600" mathvariant="normal">▲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\blacktriangle</annotation></semantics></math> Kimi K2, <math id="S6.F2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacklozenge" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#86002D;" mathcolor="#86002D" mathvariant="normal">⧫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\blacklozenge</annotation></semantics></math> Qwen 2B, <math id="S6.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\circ" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#B3B3B3;" mathcolor="#B3B3B3">∘</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\circ</annotation></semantics></math>
heuristic baselines.</figcaption>
</figure>
      
</div>
<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Qualitatively, the fine-tuned model succeeds for three recurring reasons. It
learns to isolate a single relevant hit in structured outputs such as
<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grep</span> and <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">git_log</span>; it learns to keep compact failure blocks
in noisy test, build, and service logs; and it is much better than larger
zero-shot models at returning empty output on explicit negatives. On the 59
negative examples in the held-out test set, it returns empty output 80% of the
time, compared with 7% for Qwen 35B. Its strongest
remaining failures are usually semantically adjacent selections rather than
wholly irrelevant output: the wrong file from an <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ls</span> listing, a
related commit from the same module, or a correct failure block with nearby
extra context attached. Table <a href="#S6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Setup. ‣ 6 Results ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> summarizes representative
held-out examples. Figure <a href="#S6.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Setup. ‣ 6 Results ‣ Squeez: Task-Conditioned Tool-Output Pruning for Coding Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the same behavior on a
compact <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">kubectl</span> observation, where the relevant evidence is a
two-line failure block inside a much longer output.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

exit code for the <span id="S6.F3.2.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">analytics-worker</span> container.</em></p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

full output has 250 lines; the gold evidence has two.</figcaption>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark evaluates pruning quality on single tool observations rather than
full agent trajectories. It therefore measures evidence preservation directly,
but not the downstream effect on end-to-end task completion. In addition,
usefulness is approximated with span overlap, which cannot capture every valid
alternative pruning decision. Finally, some tool families remain noisier than
others, especially <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grep</span> and <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lint_output</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Squeez is a task-conditioned tool-output pruner for coding agents. The
benchmark pairs grounded span annotations over 27 tool types with real
SWE-bench workflows and synthetic multi-ecosystem observations. A compact
LoRA-tuned Qwen 3.5 2B model reaches 0.86 recall while removing 92% of
input tokens, outperforming the 18<math id="S8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger Qwen 3.5 35B A3B and all
heuristic baselines by a wide margin. The broader lesson is that mixed-format
tool output is not handled well by zero-shot generative models or retrieval
heuristics alone; it responds well to narrow, task-specific supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The model and evaluation code are available on
<a href="https://github.com/KRLabsOrg/squeez" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">GitHub</a>, and the released model and
dataset are available on
<a href="https://huggingface.co/KRLabsOrg/squeez-2b" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Hugging Face</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">

              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
